newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: WORLD BANK DEFENDS DEBT RELIEF PLAN AS WORKABLE.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BANK DEFENDS DEBT RELIEF PLAN AS WORKABLE.

text.p: The World Bank on Wednesday defended a debt relief plan for the world's poorest countries, saying its conditions were meant to ensure governments did not reverse reforms.

Jean-Louis Sarbib and Callisto Madavo, World Bank vice presidents for the African region, told Reuters concerns raised by African finance ministers were real but they should take steps to ensure economic growth.
"We see the debt problem as real and this should be a real opportunity to make a difference," Sarbib said.
"We are not in the business of forcing a country to do something that is not in its interest. We are not police. We have travelled a long distance over this," Sarbib added.
Sarbib, Madavo, officials from Western lending groups and African ministers end a three-day conference in Addis Ababa focusing on the debt relief plan and reforms on Wednesday.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank last month approved a debt relief plan for Uganda, making it the first candidate for the Debt Initiative for Heavily Indebted Countries (HIPC).

Sarbib and Madavo said Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Bolivia were other immediate candidates for the plan. Later in the year, Madavo said, the World Bank would look at Ethiopia, Mozambique, Mali, Guinea Bissau and Sao Tome.
African ministers say criteria and eligibility for the plan are too rigid and might kill the project. They complain the World Bank fails to recognise different conditions for each country.
But Madavo said: "We would like benefiting countries to show a record of economic reforms and to show that even when HIPC expires, they will continue on the right track."
Sarbib saw hope and determination to improve lives in most of Africa and said "Africa now has a vision to move forward".
"It is for the Africans to lead, take control, and be in charge of programmes," said Madavo. "We do not want anyone to say this is a World Bank programme. They should manage it."
Africa's international debt stands at around $340 billion and Africans spend $24 billion annually on debt servicing.
The World Bank has put a $500 million contribution to an HIPC Trust Fund. Bilateral contributions stand at $43 million.

In general, a country is required under the initiative to establish a six-year record under IMF tutoring of strong economic reform efforts. Debt relief aims at improving living conditions by a sustained level of economic growth.

The initiative was undertaken when it became clear that repayment of old loans to agencies such as the World Bank and IMF were draining some of the poorest countries, making it impossible for them to get on their feet no matter what reforms they made.
"The HIPC initiative has been launched and implementation is on track. We will need to be open, review and adapt as we gain experience," Sarbib said.
